member.title: ADAPTIVE QUIZ GENERATION AND RECOMMENDATION
member.overview: The adaptive assessment component converts learning documents into grounded quizzes, evaluates submitted answers, adjusts question difficulty, and produces analytics and topic recommendations. A LangGraph workflow coordinates the agents, while SQLite stores learner-session data and checkpoints and ChromaDB stores document embeddings.

blocks: The adaptive assessment component converts learning documents into grounded quizzes, evaluates submitted answers, adjusts question difficulty, and produces analytics and topic recommendations. A LangGraph workflow coordinates the agents, while SQLite stores learner-session data and checkpoints and ChromaDB stores document embeddings.

The repository supplies a FastAPI backend, Next.js frontend, a fine-tuned Qwen Modal endpoint, and backend tests. Its README documents a deployed Modal generation URL, but live availability was not checked. No component-specific production Dockerfile, hosting manifest, or root CI/CD workflow was found. The frontend and CPU hosting arrangement below is a proposed deployment procedure based on the supplied source.

The frontend imports `@/lib/api` from quiz/upload/result pages, but `frontend/lib/api` is absent from this checkout. Restore or implement that module and validate its contracts before claiming that the frontend can be built and released.

The deployment supports assessment of a complete document-to-quiz workflow, including generation, evaluation, adaptation, hints, recommendations and session recovery. Its purpose is to establish reproducible operation of the CPU application with the fine-tuned Qwen Modal service and persistent local data.

A repeatable deployment must connect the interface, application services, model inference and persistent data while retaining the configuration and evidence required to reproduce the release. The assessment therefore considers both installation correctness and the learner-facing workflow.

This report covers the adaptive quiz generation and recommendation component only. The shared learning interface, research website and other three research components retain their own deployment responsibilities. The scope includes environment preparation, model endpoint configuration, application release, secure service access, verification, backup and recovery.

The report is based on the inspected project repository. Hosting already documented in source is identified separately from proposed installation steps. No new cloud release, paid inference or production database migration was executed during preparation. Runtime acceptance results require a release-specific evidence record.

The following metrics define the operational monitoring plan for deployment evaluation. They are selected from the component workflow and should be collected during a controlled acceptance run; measured values are not supplied in the available deployment evidence.
API /health, Modal generation failures and complete quiz requests.
Document ingestion, question generation, hints and answer-evaluation latency.
Source support, answer-type handling, difficulty changes and recommendations.
Session database, checkpoints, uploads and retrieval index after restart.

Deployment success is evaluated against installation, integration and learner workflow criteria. Health checks alone are insufficient because an API can answer a liveness request while a model, database, index or private storage service remains unavailable.
Required processes start with the selected environment and no unresolved startup failure.
Frontend origin, API URL, model endpoints and persistent paths match the release record.
All mandatory component scenarios produce the expected outcomes.
Required learner state and files remain available after a controlled restart.
A compatible previous release and tested backup procedure are identified.

For a release trial, calculate deployment success rate as successfully verified required services divided by all required services, multiplied by 100. Calculate workflow error rate from failed requests divided by total observed requests over the same recorded test interval. Keep configuration failures, model failures and invalid-input rejections separate so that expected rejection behavior is not mistaken for an outage.

No measured deployment percentage or incident trend is asserted here. The release record must identify the test period, number of requests, endpoint/model revisions, and observed failures before reporting quantitative results.

The repository review establishes the component architecture, required configuration, release dependencies, verification scenarios and recovery requirements. A completed deployment should demonstrate a usable adaptive quiz generation and recommendation workflow and durable handling of the component data described below. Operational success remains subject to the acceptance criteria and pending items identified in this report.

The deployment process follows environment preparation, initialization, application/model release, access configuration and scenario-based verification. The steps are specific to this component and preserve its actual hosting and storage architecture.
One persistent CPU service behind HTTPS
Persistent index directory; CPU model cache

The code uses SQLite and local Chroma persistence, rather than the Supabase data architecture used by some other components. A single backend instance/process is the initial deployment choice because session work, checkpoints, and local files have not been demonstrated to support multiple independent replicas.

Select the release commit and install dependencies in an isolated environment. Record the actual operating system, runtime versions, host allocation, storage mapping and public endpoints. CPU/RAM specifications and concurrent-user capacity should be taken from the selected host and measurements rather than assumed from the presence of deployment scripts.

The backend requires writable session and checkpoint database directories, an upload location and a persistent Chroma index. The graph compiles during application startup, and database service initialization creates tables and applies additive migrations. Existing state must be backed up before schema-changing releases. A single backend process is the initial deployment arrangement because multi-replica session and local-state behavior has not been demonstrated.

Configure application and model services using the following repository-supported variables and deployment sequence. Commands use a Linux deployment shell unless a PowerShell helper is explicitly identified.

Use an isolated Python environment and `backend/requirements.txt`. Python 3.11 matches the Modal inference image; validate the CPU requirements in a clean environment before selecting the host runtime. The frontend package metadata takes precedence over the README's older Next.js 14 description.
Generation endpoint; default documented in component README
Optional authorization value sent by the backend client
Model request timeout; source default 45 seconds
Production origin added to backend CORS allowlist
Public browser API URL, configured before frontend build
Set false to avoid debug logging/reload through the script entry point

Set persistent paths relative to a fixed backend working directory or use absolute persistent paths. The Modal endpoint requires the existing `huggingface-secret` containing `HF_TOKEN`. It caches `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` and the adapter `Nishy11/nishy-qwen2.5-7b-v4` during image construction.

1. Record the release commit, restore the missing frontend API module, and review its request/response types against backend routers. Validate dependency compatibility, especially the installed LangGraph and checkpoint packages.
2. Authenticate Modal, provision its Hugging Face secret privately, and deploy from the component backend:

Record the returned endpoint and configure `MODAL_ENDPOINT_URL`. The model uses an A10G GPU, a 600-second function timeout, and a 600-second scaledown window in source. These are configuration values, not measured release latency.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
Populate the private `.env` from `.env.example`. Create/persist the database parent directories, upload directory, and embedding cache. Set `FRONTEND_URL` to the exact hosted origin.
4. Configure a process manager to run the following from the backend working directory, behind an HTTPS reverse proxy:

Use a single worker initially and no reload option. Startup compiles the graph; database service initialization creates tables and performs additive migrations. Back up existing state before introducing a version that changes its schema.
5. From `frontend/`, configure `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` to the HTTPS API origin and run:

npm ci
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run build
npm run start

The final command applies to a managed Node server. An independent Next.js hosting project can run the same build without a local persistent frontend process. The missing API module must be fixed first. Rebuild after public API URL changes; the configured default is localhost.

6. Expose only the intended HTTPS application endpoints. Keep database, vector index, and document files outside public web roots. Record the selected host, process-manager configuration, and persistent-volume mapping in the release record.

The hosted browser interface and API require compatible HTTPS endpoints and exact permitted frontend origins. Private credentials belong in the backend or deployment-secret store. Public frontend variables may contain the API origin and public identity key, but must not contain database passwords, service-role credentials or private deployment tokens.

Restrict internal process and database/index ports to the required application network. Access control must match the intended audience and be verified independently of CORS. Record how an administrator inspects logs and restarts the service using the tools selected for this component.

Execute the following component-specific scenarios using isolated test accounts, representative source material and a recorded release configuration. The descriptions are acceptance procedures, not claims that the scenarios have already passed.
2.5.1 Scenario 1 - Document ingestion and grounded quiz
Test procedure: Upload a supported document, create a session and inspect generated questions with their source context.
Expected behavior: Questions follow the supplied material and rejected/unsupported generation is handled explicitly.
Evidence to retain: request/test identifier, relevant screenshot or response, timestamps, service/model version and the observed pass/fail outcome.
Test procedure: Submit correct and incorrect examples for both supported answer types and inspect feedback.
Expected behavior: Evaluation is returned through the intended route and the session records the submitted answer.
Evidence to retain: request/test identifier, relevant screenshot or response, timestamps, service/model version and the observed pass/fail outcome.
Test procedure: Advance through questions with different performance patterns, request hints and view final recommendations.
Expected behavior: Difficulty and recommendations reflect the implemented session logic, with usable learner feedback.
Evidence to retain: request/test identifier, relevant screenshot or response, timestamps, service/model version and the observed pass/fail outcome.
2.5.4 Scenario 4 - Restart, checkpoints and model timeout
Test procedure: Restart during an isolated session and simulate an unavailable model endpoint.
Expected behavior: Session/checkpoint state is retained and model failure produces an understandable outcome.
Evidence to retain: request/test identifier, relevant screenshot or response, timestamps, service/model version and the observed pass/fail outcome.

Back up SQLite using a consistent database backup mechanism or while writes are stopped; do not copy only a live `.db` file while ignoring journal/WAL state. Back up session data, checkpoints, uploads, and Chroma index as a compatible set. Verify restoration in an isolated environment.

Monitor model timeouts, queue/session processing, failed questions, disk usage, SQLite contention, and retrieval errors. Local embedding weights need cache space and initial download access. Measure concurrent sessions before increasing capacity. Multiple replicas require a deliberate redesign of shared state and background work; they are not established by the current setup.

Keep the previous frontend build, backend release/environment, and model adapter reference. Restore compatible application code and model routing independently. If additive database changes make the old release incompatible, use a reviewed migration plan or restore from a consistent backup while accounting for subsequent learner data. Repeat upload, answer, and persistence checks after rollback.

Deployment is complete only when required services and dependencies are reachable, the interface uses the intended API, persistent storage is retained, and mandatory scenarios pass with evidence. Record any unresolved issue as a release limitation. The current report provides a verification procedure and source-based readiness assessment; it does not replace operator sign-off.

These actions must be verified in the release environment. Their presence in this report does not mean the corresponding source code, host configuration or production installation was modified during report preparation.

Configuration and build gaps can prevent a usable client release even when individual backend services exist. Missing model artifacts or mismatched endpoints can interrupt inference, while incomplete persistence can cause learner state or feedback loss after restart. The listed actions address these concrete release dependencies. No outage duration, user count or production incident severity is inferred without a live record.

Collect application logs, process status, model-platform logs and persistent-storage usage for the selected deployment. Correlate API and model events using request/job/session identifiers wherever available. Inspect both total request duration and individual processing stages, since a slow or unavailable dependency can be hidden by an otherwise responsive API.

Use the metrics in Section 1.4 for a consistent monitoring record. Separate startup/liveness checks from full workflow checks, and retain cold-start observations alongside warm-request behavior. No additional monitoring dashboard is claimed to be installed by this report.
Reviewed and described in this report.

Requires verification in an isolated environment.

No new deployment user-feedback study was supplied or conducted for this report. Collect feedback after the component scenarios using the intended learner audience. Record whether users can complete the workflow, understand errors, interpret results and recover their prior work. Keep reported comments and participant counts separate from proposed usability improvements.
4. POST-DEPLOYMENT VALIDATION, DOCUMENTATION, AND LESSONS LEARNED

Post-deployment validation checks the integrated learning workflow after the selected release is installed. The procedure covers infrastructure, application dependencies, interface behavior and persistence. Validation should use representative learning material and controlled test state rather than modifying real learner records for convenience.

Install the backend test runner separately if it is not present; it is not listed in the runtime requirements. From the backend environment, run `python -m pytest tests/` using isolated test state. Run frontend TypeScript and production build checks after restoring its API module.

Check `/health` and then a full document-to-quiz flow: upload a supported document, create a session, generate questions with source grounding, submit MCQ/open-ended answers, request a hint where supported, advance, and view results/recommendations. Restart the service and verify persistence of sessions, source documents, vector index, and graph checkpoints.

Test unavailable model responses and timeout behavior. `/health` returns a static healthy response and does not check database or Modal availability. Successful deployment requires real workflow evidence in addition to liveness.
Record actual test results, release commit, model/adapter version, persistent paths, hosted frontend/API URLs, and acceptance date. No pass/fail runtime results were collected for this report.
Inspect process/container status, HTTPS endpoint reachability, persistent mounts and startup logs.
Verify dependency configuration, model response handling, error behavior and the component-specific scenarios.
Validate the hosted production build, uploads/actions, result display and learner-visible failure behavior.
Restart services, confirm state retention, inspect access boundaries and verify compatible restoration.

Retain the source commit, runtime/package manifests, environment-variable names, deployment scripts/configuration, model identifiers, schema versions, test output and scenario evidence with the release. Store private environment values outside the published report. The editable report source and rendered PDF provide the documentation layer; application artefacts remain in the component directory.
The following source-based limitations and supporting references remain relevant to release sign-off:

Pending items are the missing frontend API module, validated dependency installation/build, production CPU/frontend hosts, durable-disk provisioning, release automation, and live acceptance evidence. Authentication and learner-data access controls must be assessed for the intended hosting audience; this report does not establish an authenticated production deployment.

The following lessons are derived from implementation and deployment review. They describe engineering implications of the available source, rather than unrecorded user trials or production performance claims.
Persistent state is part of the assessment deployment, not an incidental local development file.
A static health response must be complemented by a complete quiz and evaluation scenario.
Horizontal scaling requires shared-state and background-work design beyond the current single-instance setup.
A report should distinguish the installed architecture, planned checks and measured results so that later releases remain auditable.

The deployment review establishes a component-specific architecture, reproducible installation sequence, verification scenarios, monitoring plan and recovery requirements for adaptive quiz generation and recommendation. The identified pending items must be resolved and the acceptance evidence recorded before certifying a successful live deployment. The supporting documentation provides a reproducible operational basis for component evaluation and future releases.
